functions.description: Read a configuration by id. Expands ${VAR:default} placeholders against the live process env unless raw=true is passed.
List every registered configuration with id, name, description, and schema. Sorted by id; never returns the stored value.

Register a configuration id with a name, description, and JSON Schema. Idempotent — re-registering replaces metadata and (when initial_value is provided) the value. Validates initial_value against the schema.
Retrieve the schema, name, and description for a configuration id. Mirrors a single entry from configuration::list.
Replace the value of an already-registered configuration. Validates the value against the registered JSON Schema and emits a configuration:updated event.
Estimate token usage for a set of messages (+ optional invocation schemas / system prompt) vs a model.
Replace verbose function outputs with placeholders without summarising. A cheaper first pass before compaction.
Internal: reload cron configuration from the authoritative store on change.
Open an interactive transaction; returns a handle to use with transactionQuery/transactionExecute/commitTransaction/rollbackTransaction.

Read a table page by page with typed filters and sorts, without writing SQL. Filters are structured (column, op, value) and compile to a parameterised WHERE for the driver in hand; the total honours the same filters. Use an equality filter at page_size 1 to follow a foreign key.

Profile a table's columns. Reads the planner's own statistics by default, which is free and approximate; `exact` runs real aggregates and scans the table. To profile rows you already hold, pipe a browseTable result through the fp worker instead.
Commit and finalize an interactive transaction.
Delete a saved query by id or by name.

Describe every table at once — the same shape as describeTable, but one catalog query per aspect across the whole database instead of one call per table. Use this to reason about relationships; set include_indexes only when you need them.

Describe one table or view: columns with type, nullability, default, primary-key membership and foreign-key target; plus indexes and a planner row estimate. Foreign keys are structured (schema, table, column), not a joined string.
Run a write statement (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL).
Run an ordered batch of SQL statements atomically (bare strings or {sql, params} objects); rolls back on first failure.

Return a statement's query plan as a tree with per-node costs, row estimates and warnings, instead of the driver's raw text. `analyze` collects real timings by RUNNING the statement, so it defaults to false and is refused for anything that is not a single read.

How a table is laid out for reading: column widths, hidden columns and column order. Stored in the state worker rather than a browser, so it survives a restart and any caller can set it up for someone else.

Live pool occupancy plus active queries, table sizes, blocking locks and cache hit ratio. Each section reports separately as available, unsupported or denied, so a driver gap or a restricted role is never mistaken for an empty result.

Recent queries run against a database, newest first. Best effort — recording never blocks or fails a query, so this is a convenience rather than an audit log. For an audit trail bind database::row-changed.
List all configured databases with connection details (driver, credential-redacted URL, pool settings, TLS mode). Config only — no health checks or live pool statistics.
List the saved queries for a database, sorted by name.
List every table and view in a database, with its kind and (on postgres) its schema. Reads the driver's own catalog, so no dialect-specific SQL is needed from the caller.
Internal: reload connection pools from the authoritative configuration when it changes.
Prepare a parameterized statement once.
Run a read-only SQL query and return the result rows.
Rollback and finalize an interactive transaction.
Run a previously-prepared handle.
Save a named query against a database. Stored in the state worker, so it survives restarts and an agent can save one for a human to find in the console. Saving under an existing name replaces it.

Replace the stored layout for a table. Widths are clamped to a usable range; columns the table no longer has are kept rather than rejected, so a rename degrades to a missing width instead of an error.

Lay out the schema as a diagram: positioned table nodes and routed foreign-key edges, plus the hub degree of each table, the isolated tables, and the remaining edge crossings. Reads the whole catalog in a handful of queries rather than one per table.
Terminate a backend session, or cancel just its running statement with `cancel_only`. Takes an id from database::health. Separate from health because it is a write.
Probe a candidate database config (url + optional tls) with one throwaway connection, without touching configured pools. Reports ok/driver/latency/server version; failures are data, not errors.
Run a sequence of statements atomically.
Run a write statement inside an interactive transaction. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK are rejected; use commit/rollbackTransaction.
Run a read-only SQL query inside an interactive transaction.
Full detail for one engine function: schemas, owning worker, and registered triggers that target it. Proxies to the engine's native engine::functions::info for the core data.
Fetch one filesystem-backed prompt by name. Returns the raw markdown body plus name, description, and modified_at — no envelope, no templating.
List filesystem-backed prompts (name, description, modified_at) from skills_folder.

Overwrite one EXISTING filesystem-backed prompt with new full-file markdown content. The frontmatter must keep a non-empty `description` (and a valid `name` when it declares one) — the same rules the scanner enforces, so an update can never produce a file the next directory::prompts::list would skip. The write is atomic and fans out directory::prompts::on-change with { op: "update" }. Returns the prompt's effective name after the write (frontmatter `name:` wins over the file stem).

Fetch full registry metadata for one worker: worker envelope (same core fields as the engine's `engine::workers::list` row shape, plus registry-only `type` / `config` / `supported_targets` / `total_downloads` / `dependencies` / `image`), readme, full API reference (functions + triggers schemas), and the tree of skill / prompt file paths fetched from the registry's /w/{slug}/skills endpoint. Pass either `version` or `tag` (defaults to tag="latest"). Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms`.

List workers from the public registry (api.workers.iii.dev). Optional free-text `search` is matched fuzzily by the registry; omit it to browse by `total_downloads DESC`. Pagination is cursor-based with a server-authored page size — pass back `pagination.next_cursor` as `cursor` to fetch the next page. Shares the core `name` / `description` / `version` fields with the engine's `engine::workers::list`. Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms` (default 60s).

Download skills + prompts into skills_folder from EITHER source. Prefer the explicit directory::skills::download_from_registry / directory::skills::download_from_repo, whose schemas can't be mixed up. Pass {repo, skill, branch?} to clone one skill folder from a GitHub repo (branch defaults to "main"), or {worker, version?|tag?} to pull from the workers registry (tag defaults to "latest"). Specify exactly ONE source set. Files in the destination namespace are overwritten file-by-file.

Download one worker's skills + prompts from the workers registry into skills_folder. `worker` is required; pass either `version` (exact semver) OR `tag` (e.g. "latest", the default when both are omitted), not both. Files in the destination namespace are overwritten file-by-file. A missing worker returns a `D310 not_found` naming the next function to call. To pull from a GitHub repo instead, use directory::skills::download_from_repo.

Download one skill folder from a GitHub repo into skills_folder. `repo` (the repo URL) and `skill` (the subfolder under `skills/`, which also names the destination namespace) are required; `branch` defaults to "main". The repo URL is validated (https / ssh / git@ only). To pull a published worker instead, use directory::skills::download_from_registry.

Fetch one filesystem-backed skill by id and return its raw markdown body plus id, title, type, function_id, and modified_at. A worker overview is addressed by the bare worker name (e.g. "iii-sandbox") — that is the id `list`/`index` hand back. Input is forgiving: "iii-sandbox/index", "iii-sandbox/SKILL.md", a trailing ".md", and an iii:// prefix all resolve to the same overview; and if the exact id misses, the worker name is matched case-insensitively as a substring ("sandbox" finds "iii-sandbox"). `title` prefers frontmatter `title:` over the body H1; `type` is the frontmatter `type:`. There is no `description` field here (the body already opens with that paragraph) — use directory::skills::list for the teaser-only view. On a miss you get a `D110 not_found` message naming the closest ids and the next function to call.

Render a per-WORKER overview: one short markdown block per installed worker (each worker's root overview doc `<ns>/index`, whether or not it declares frontmatter `type: index`). Each block is a `## <worker title>` heading, the first paragraph of that worker's overview, and a `directory::skills::get` call to read the full reference. Token-light by design and intended for system-prompt injection; for individual per-SKILL rows call directory::skills::list.

List skills as one row PER SKILL (id, title, type, function_id, description, bytes, modified_at) from skills_folder — use this when you need individual skill ids. A worker overview row's `id` is the bare worker name (e.g. `iii-sandbox`); pass it straight to directory::skills::get. For a per-WORKER overview instead, call directory::skills::index. Filters: `search` (case-insens. substring vs id+title+description), `prefix` (worker-namespace prefix; matches the overview row and its sub-skills), `type` (exact frontmatter type match). Pass `include_description: false` for token-light id+title+type rows (default: descriptions included). `title` prefers frontmatter `title:` over the body H1. Each row's `function_id` is the callable bus id (e.g. `sandbox::create`) — pass THAT to agent_trigger, not the row's `id` (which is a documentation address).

Overwrite one EXISTING filesystem-backed skill with new full-file markdown content (frontmatter block included — pass back the `raw` field from directory::skills::get { raw: true }, edited). Accepts the same id forms as `get`. Never creates files (use directory::skills::download to materialize a bundle). Content is validated against the read invariants (size cap, non-empty body after frontmatter); the write is atomic and fans out directory::skills::on-change with { op: "update" }.
Browse DLQ messages
List DLQ topics with counts
Internal provider for TriggerAction::Enqueue
List all queue topics
Get stats for a queue topic

Remove null elements from an array (lodash _.compact, null-only: 0, false and "" are KEPT so plucked data survives): { value }. Pairs with fp::map, whose sporadic misses become null. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Trigger-binding guard: compare a JSON pointer inside the fired event and answer the condition contract ({ decision: "allow" | "skip", reason }). Config is { path?, op, to?, negate? } with the fp::when ops (==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty); a pointer that resolves to nothing SKIPS rather than erroring, so "not there yet" is an ordinary answer. Use it as a binding's `conditions` entry so a reaction fires only on events that matter — it is not a fan-in gate (that is state::barrier), it filters one event at a time.

Count array elements per plucked key (lodash _.countBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": <count> } (`""` counts by the element itself). Same key rules as fp::groupBy. Pair with fp::groupBy + fp::sum for a per-key total. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Skip the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.drop): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Keep array elements whose properties equal a partial object (lodash _.filter with a matches iteratee): { value, matches: { status: "active" } }. matches is a partial OBJECT (never a bare string/number) and only object elements can match. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Flatten an array one level (lodash _.flatten): [1,[2],[[3]]] -> [1,2,[3]]. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the single value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.get): { value, path: "/content" }. A miss names the keys that were available. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the value at a JSON pointer, or `default` when the path misses (lodash fp.getOr): { value, path, default }. A stored null is a hit, not a miss. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Bucket array elements by a plucked key (lodash _.groupBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": [element, ...] } (`""` groups by the element itself). Keys must be a string, number, or boolean; a null or container key errors rather than collapsing distinct groups into one bucket. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Join array elements into one string (lodash _.join): { value, separator } (separator defaults to ","). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Pluck the value at a JSON pointer from each array element (lodash _.map with a property iteratee): { value, path: "/id" }. Sporadic misses become null (fp::compact drops them), but a path matching NO element errors — pointers pluck stored fields, not computed properties like /length (fp::size counts). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Largest number in an array (lodash _.max/_.maxBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.maxBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Arithmetic mean of an array of numbers (lodash _.mean/_.meanBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/score" }. Deviates from lodash: an EMPTY array errors instead of yielding NaN, which would thread garbage into the next step. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Smallest number in an array (lodash _.min/_.minBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.minBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Element at index n; negative n counts from the end (lodash _.nth): { value, n: -1 } is the last element. Out of bounds errors naming the length. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Drop top-level keys from an object (lodash _.omit): { value, paths: ["a","b"] }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Subset an object by top-level keys (lodash _.pick): { value, paths: ["a","b"] } -> {a, b}; missing keys are omitted. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.
Reverse an array (lodash _.reverse, immutable like lodash/fp): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Count a collection (lodash _.size): array length, string chars, or object key count: { value }. Non-collections error instead of returning 0. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Sort array elements ascending by the value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.sortBy, stable): { value, path } — path "" sorts the elements themselves (primitives). Keys must all be numbers, strings, or booleans; an element missing the path errors. Pair with fp::reverse for descending. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Split a string into an array of strings (lodash _.split): { value, separator: "\n" }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Total an array of numbers (lodash _.sum/_.sumBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" } to pluck the addend from each element first. An empty array totals 0; a non-numeric element errors rather than being skipped. All-integer inputs total to an integer, so the result compares cleanly in a fp::when guard. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Keep the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.take): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Deduplicate an array, keeping first occurrences (lodash _.uniq): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Guard: test the value at a JSON pointer ({ value, path?, op, to? }; ops ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty; path defaults to the whole value; a pointer miss FAILS the guard, it never errors). Dry-run validation of an iii.worker.yaml WITHOUT installing anything. Pass `manifest` (inline YAML text) or `path` (host file/dir). Returns errors, unknown keys, deprecated keys, and warnings — author, validate, then worker::add.

content.text:
Key findings:
- `database` worker with `database::row-changed` trigger type: "Fires after this worker commits a row change, filtered by `db`, optional `table`, and optional `ops`. Reports only mutations made THROUGH this worker — not change data capture."
- Database functions: query, execute, executeBatch, transaction, browseTable, describeTable, listDatabases, etc.
- `harness::spawn` for sub-agents.
- No `state` functions granted (the requirement says state functions are not granted — I shouldn't use state worker).

The plan:
1. Check database setup: list databases to find `primary`, list tables to see what exists.
2. Design mechanics:
   - Ledger maintenance: The requirement says "Maintain a live ledger in database `primary` — per supplier: shipment count and total value — kept current as data lands WITHOUT running a model turn for each change." Options:
     a. Database triggers (native SQL triggers) — but wait, the database worker is SQLite/Postgres/MySQL. Database triggers in SQL would update the ledger automatically. But the requirement says "database `primary` plus trigger machinery on top of it" — trigger machinery on top of the database. Hmm, "The ONLY shared medium in this run is database `primary` plus trigger machinery on top of it."
     b. engine::register_trigger with `database::row-changed` trigger type, calling a plain function (deterministic, token-free) that updates the ledger. This is "trigger machinery on top of it" — the trigger fires on row changes and calls a function to update the ledger. This avoids model turns per change.
     
     The `database::row-changed` trigger fires after a row change made through this worker, filtered by db, optional table, optional ops. So I could register a trigger that fires on insert into `receiving_d67d641f_shipments` and calls a function to update the ledger.

     But wait — the trigger calls a function `function_id` — "any plain function your policy allows" with metadata payload. The function would need to update the ledger: upsert count and total per supplier. That function would be a registered function... but do I have a worker that has such a function? I'd need to write a worker to register a function like `receiving::update_ledger` that, given a supplier and value, updates the ledger (increment count and total). That's a lot of work.

     Alternatively, use a native database trigger (SQL) — but the requirement says trigger machinery on top of the database. Actually, using SQL database triggers would be the most natural: "Maintain a live ledger ... kept current as data lands" — a SQL trigger on shipments that updates the ledger. But then "Learn that the whole run is complete FROM THE DATABASE ITSELF" — the completion signal is a row in `receiving_d67d641f_completion`. The `database::row-changed` engine trigger can fire when that row is inserted, and wake me exactly once.

     Hmm, but there's a subtlety: `database::row-changed` reports "only mutations made THROUGH this worker — not change data capture." So if couriers write via `database::execute`/`database::transaction`, those go through the database worker, so the trigger would fire. Good.

     But if we use native SQL triggers to maintain the ledger, those are in the database and fire regardless. Then the ledger maintenance happens without any model turn. And the completion wake uses `database::row-changed` engine trigger on the completion table, waking me once.

     Actually wait — would the SQL trigger's internal writes (INSERT into ledger) also fire `database::row-changed`? The trigger says "Reports only mutations made THROUGH this worker". Internal SQL-trigger mutations might be reported too (they're made through the worker's connection). That could cause extra fires, but if I filter by table = completion table, only completion row insert fires. For the ledger maintenance, if done via SQL triggers, no engine trigger needed.

     Let me think about which approach is cleaner:

     Approach A: Native SQL triggers maintain the ledger.
     - CREATE TRIGGER after INSERT on shipments: upsert ledger (increment count, add value).
     - Also the correction (+1.0 to seq-2 shipment): couriers UPDATE the shipments row value = value + 1.0. That should also update the ledger. So need an UPDATE trigger too (or make the courier write the corrected value in a way that... no, the correction is applied after recording). Actually the courier records three shipments, then applies a correction (+1.0 to its seq-2 shipment). The correction modifies the shipments row. The ledger should reflect the final state: acme: 10 + (5+1) + 3 = 19.0. Yes! The expected totals include the correction: acme 3 / 19.0 = 10 + 6 + 3. globex: 7.5 + (2.5+1) + 4 = 15.0. initech: 6 + (8+1) + 1 = 16.0. So ledger must reflect corrections.
     - So SQL triggers on INSERT and UPDATE of shipments that adjust the ledger accordingly. For UPDATE: decrement old value, add new value. For INSERT: add value, increment count. (No deletes.)
     - This maintains the ledger without any model turn. 
     
     But is "database trigger machinery" allowed? "The ONLY shared medium in this run is database `primary` plus trigger machinery on top of it." Yes — triggers are explicitly part of the allowed machinery. And "cleanup means retiring bindings and database triggers" — that confirms database triggers are expected to be created ("database triggers" are explicitly mentioned in cleanup: "cleanup means retiring bindings and database triggers, not deleting the evidence tables"). So the intended design uses BOTH engine bindings AND database triggers.

     Approach B: Engine `database::row-changed` triggers call a plain function to update the ledger. That would require writing a worker with a function that does the upsert. More moving parts.

     Approach A is simpler and matches "without running a model turn for each change" perfectly — SQL triggers run in the DB engine. And the completion wake uses the engine `database::row-changed` trigger on the completion table waking me once (wake-me shape, omit function_id, once: true).

     Wait, but there's a subtlety with Approach A: when the courier inserts into shipments via `database::execute`, the SQL trigger updates the ledger. The engine `database::row-changed` trigger would ALSO fire for the shipments insert (mutations through the worker) and the ledger update (also through the worker?). If I bind `database::row-changed` filtered to table=completion, only completion inserts fire. Good.

     Then the completion row: who writes it? The couriers each signal finished by updating `receiving_d67d641f_couriers` status = 'done'. The completion row should be written when all three are done — "completion signal: `receiving_d67d641f_completion` (exactly one row when the run is complete)".

     How to write exactly one completion row when all three couriers are done? A database trigger! SQL: after UPDATE on couriers, check if all three have status 'done' (or count where status='done' = 3), and if so, insert into completion... but "exactly one row" — need to guard against multiple inserts. Use INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS, or a trigger that only inserts when count(*) == 3 and no row exists yet.

     But wait — the completion row must be written through the database worker for the engine `database::row-changed` trigger on the completion table to fire ("Reports only mutations made THROUGH this worker"). A native SQL trigger inserting into completion happens within a statement executed through the worker, so it is a mutation made through the worker — I believe the row-changed trigger would see it. Actually, hmm. The row-changed trigger type description says "Fires after this worker commits a row change... Reports only mutations made THROUGH this worker — not change data capture." Native SQL triggers executing inside the worker's statement execution are still mutations made through the worker's connection/statement. The engine likely hooks into the driver's statement execution results and reports affected rows. Native triggers may or may not be captured. Risky.

     Alternative: let the completion insert be done by the last courier? But couriers shouldn't coordinate. Hmm.

     Alternative: The engine `database::row-changed` trigger can be bound with a condition — e.g., `fp::condition` as a gate. But a condition filters one event at a time; it's not a fan-in across three different events... Actually there's `state::barrier` but that's a state condition (state functions not granted — well, conditions are functions; state::barrier would be a state function... "State functions are not granted" — the condition itself being state::barrier means state worker is used. Not allowed? The requirement says state functions are not granted — meaning I don't have access to call state functions. Conditions use function ids — if state::barrier isn't in my allowed list, it would be refused. Let me not use it.)

     Let me think about the completion detection differently:
     - Each courier writes status='done' in couriers table.
     - A native SQL trigger after UPDATE on couriers: when all 3 rows are 'done' and completion table empty, insert completion row. But will the engine row-changed trigger on completion fire for that? Uncertain.
     
     Safer: I (root) bind the `database::row-changed` trigger filtered to table=couriers, op=UPDATE, waking me once, but I need to only wake when ALL three are done, ideally exactly once. The requirement: "Learn that the whole run is complete FROM THE DATABASE ITSELF, waking as few times as possible — ideally exactly once — and never by polling."

     Options for exactly-once wake:
     a. Bind row-changed on completion table (wake once when completion row inserted). The completion row is written by a native SQL trigger. Risk: native trigger insert may not be captured by the engine's row-changed detection. Need to verify.
     b. Bind row-changed on couriers table with a condition function that checks the DB whether all three are done... conditions are functions answering { decision: "allow" | "skip" }. The condition function would need to query the database (database::query is a plain function) and decide allow only when all three couriers are done. That would be a "call a function" binding... no wait, conditions can be used with wake-me bindings? The docs: "conditions: [{ function_id, config? }] — gates evaluated in order before delivery." And for wake-me shape: "The event arrives as a message in THIS session and starts a turn." Conditions apply to delivery. So a wake-me binding with a condition: event fires on each courier status update; condition checks DB (via a function) whether all 3 are done; if yes → allow → wake me once (once: true). If not → skip → no wake. That gives exactly one wake!
     
     But the condition function must be a registered function I can call... The condition `function_id` is "an ordinary function answering { decision: "allow" | "skip", payload?, reason? }". I'd need to write a worker that registers such a function. That's worker authoring — significant but doable. Actually, is there an existing function that can do this? `fp::condition` is a comparison guard on the event payload — it can't query the database. Hmm.

     Alternatively: The condition could check the event payload itself! What does `database::row-changed` deliver? Probably something like { db, table, op, rows: [...] } or similar. Let me check the trigger type's schema via engine::triggers::info.

     Actually, another idea: I could bind row-changed on couriers (wake me, once: false is default for wake... default wake is once) — but I want exactly once total when the run completes, not per courier. 

     Let me think about the cleanest design given constraints:

     Constraint: "Learn that the whole run is complete FROM THE DATABASE ITSELF, waking as few times as possible — ideally exactly once — and never by polling."

     The completion table exists for this: "completion signal: `receiving_d67d641f_completion` (exactly one row when the run is complete)". So the intended flow: someone writes exactly one row into completion when all couriers are done; I bind a wake on completion row insertion (exactly once). 

     Who writes the completion row? Since couriers are minimal-privilege and don't coordinate, the completion row should be written by... the database itself (SQL trigger) or by a trigger-machinery function. "The ONLY shared medium in this run is database `primary` plus trigger machinery on top of it." — "trigger machinery on top of it" suggests engine triggers calling plain functions. So maybe: an engine trigger on couriers status updates calls a plain function (deterministic, no model turn) that checks whether all three couriers are done and, if so, writes the completion row (exactly once via a guard). That function would be a registered function — again requires worker authoring.

     Hmm wait — maybe I can use `fp::pipe` as the trigger target function! "Call a function — function_id: '<any function your policy allows>' with metadata: { payload: {...}, event_into: '/event' }". fp::pipe is a plain function. So I could bind row-changed on couriers → call fp::pipe which: queries couriers, counts done, and if 3, inserts into completion. But fp::pipe's `fp::when` guard stops the pipe on failure, so a trailing write (database::execute insert completion) runs only when condition holds. 

     The pipe would be:
     - step 1: database::query { db: "primary", sql: "SELECT COUNT(*) AS done FROM couriers WHERE status='done'" } — wait, but each step's result lands in the next step's payload at into. The first step's payload must be a producing function. database::query payload: { db, sql, params? }.
     - step 2: fp::get { path: "/rows/0/done" } — extract the count. Need to know query response shape.
     - step 3: fp::when { op: "==", to: 3 } — wait, but fp::when threads the ORIGINAL value onward unchanged when passing. The original value here would be the count (after fp::get). Hmm, actually fp::when tests the value at path (default whole value) and threads the original value onward. If I get the count first via fp::get, then fp::when { op: "==", to: 3 } passes only when count==3, threading count=3 onward.
     - step 4: database::execute { db, sql: "INSERT INTO completion ..." } — but I need to ensure exactly one row. functions.description: List all configured databases with connection details (driver, credential-redacted URL, pool settings, TLS mode). Config only — no health checks or live pool statistics.

PoolInfo.description: Pool settings echoed back from config (no live stats).

TlsInfo.description: TLS settings. `ca_cert` is reported as a presence boolean only — never the path, which would leak filesystem layout.

oneOf.description: No TLS. Plaintext connection. Local-dev only.
TLS handshake required; certificate chain validated; hostname NOT verified. Matches libpq's `sslmode=require`. The default.
TLS handshake required; certificate chain validated; certificate hostname must match the URL host. Matches libpq's `sslmode=verify-full`.

functions.description: List every table and view in a database, with its kind and (on postgres) its schema. Reads the driver's own catalog, so no dialect-specific SQL is needed from the caller.

db.description: Logical database name. Optional — omitting it targets the sole configured database, or `primary` when several are configured.

TableRef.description: A relation. `schema` is populated only where the driver has a meaningful namespace above the table (postgres); it is never concatenated into `name`, because `analytics.events` and a table literally called `analytics.events` are different things and callers must be able to tell them apart.

functions.description: Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.

AgentMessage.description: The canonical transcript message union. Untagged: the single-variant role tags disambiguate deserialization (assistant/function_result/custom are tried before user so their required fields gate the match).

oneOf.description: Opaque redacted thinking payload — replayed verbatim on the wire.

ExposeMode.description: How allowed functions reach the model (harness.md § Exposure modes).

FunctionPolicy.description: The fail-closed dispatch policy (harness.md § Functions). Absent on the send => every call denied (a plain chat loop).

Mode.description: Console / send operating mode — prepends a short paragraph before the shared identity prompt. `ask` is also structural: the turn's dispatch policy is capped at the configured default policy, never widened.

filesystem_root.description: Absolute filesystem root for the child turn (e.g. an isolated `worktree::create` checkout), written to the child's `metadata.fs_scope.root`. When set it overrides the inherited scope for this child; when absent the child inherits its direct parent's root unchanged.

functions.description: Intersected with the parent policy — narrow, never escalate. An `ask`-mode child is further capped at the configured default policy.

max_children.description: Fan-out guard for the child's own spawns.

content.text:
Now I understand the contracts. Let me now inspect the database itself:
1. database::listDatabases — find `primary`, driver.
2. database::listTables — see existing tables.

Key facts so far:
- `database::row-changed` trigger: config { db (required), table? (case-insensitive match), ops? (insert/update/delete/other) }. Event: { affected_rows, at, db, op, returning?, table? }.
- `database::query` response: { columns, row_count, rows }.
- `database::execute`: { db?, params?, returning?, sql }.
- `database::transaction`: { db?, isolation?, statements: [{sql, params?}] } → atomic.
- `harness::spawn`: { task, session_id?, options: { functions: { allow: [...] }, ... } }. Child is leaf; narrowed functions via options.functions.allow.
- `engine::register_trigger`: { trigger_type, config, function_id?, metadata?, once?, lifecycle?, label?, conditions? }.
- `engine::unregister_trigger`: { id }.
- `harness::triggers::list` / `harness::triggers::unregister`: { subscription_id }.

Design decision time. Let me look at the DB first. Let me call listDatabases and listTables.
Contracts are clear. Now let me inspect the actual database `primary` — driver, existing tables, and schema state.

{"count":1,"databases":[{"driver":"sqlite","name":"primary","pool":{"acquire_timeout_ms":5000,"idle_timeout_ms":30000,"max":10},"tls":{"ca_cert_present":false,"mode":"require","trust_native":true},"url":"sqlite:/home/runner/work/workers/workers/target/harness-e2e/stack/database/iii.db"}]}
{"count":0,"tables":[]}

The database is SQLite (`sqlite:/home/runner/work/workers/workers/target/harness-e2e/stack/database/iii.db`). No tables yet — I need to create all four result relations plus any machinery.

SQLite supports CREATE TRIGGER and UPSERT (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, since 3.24 — modern SQLite).

Now let me design the full mechanics:

## Schema (SQLite)

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS receiving_d67d641f_shipments (
  supplier TEXT NOT NULL,
  seq INTEGER NOT NULL,
  value REAL NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (supplier, seq)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS receiving_d67d641f_ledger (
  supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  shipment_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
  total_value REAL NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS receiving_d67d641f_couriers (
  supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  status TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS receiving_d67d641f_completion (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1),
  completed_at TEXT NOT NULL
);
```

For the completion table, "exactly one row" — enforce with `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id = 1)` so only one row can exist (second insert → PK conflict).

## Ledger maintenance — native SQL triggers

Option 1: native SQL triggers:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS receiving_d67d641f_ledger_ins
AFTER INSERT ON receiving_d67d641f_shipments
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO receiving_d67d641f_ledger (supplier, shipment_count, total_value)
  VALUES (NEW.supplier, 1, NEW.value)
  ON CONFLICT(supplier) DO UPDATE SET
    shipment_count = shipment_count + 1,
    total_value = total_value + NEW.value;
END;

CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS receiving_d67d641f_ledger_upd
AFTER UPDATE OF value ON receiving_d67d641f_shipments
BEGIN
  UPDATE receiving_d67d641f_ledger
  SET total_value = total_value - OLD.value + NEW.value
  WHERE supplier = NEW.supplier;
END;
```

Wait — a subtlety: the AFTER UPDATE OF value trigger fires on value changes. When the courier corrects seq-2, it does UPDATE shipments SET value = value + 1.0 WHERE supplier=? AND seq=2. That fires the update trigger: total_value -= old, += new. 

But wait — is the ledger guaranteed to have a row at that point? Yes, the insert trigger created it.

Also: what if a courier updates the value before... no, couriers insert then update. Fine.

Option 2: engine-trigger recompute. I decided native triggers for the ledger — atomic with data, zero async machinery, exactly "kept current as data lands". The task explicitly mentions "database triggers" in cleanup, so native triggers are expected.

But hold on — one concern with native triggers: does the engine's `database::row-changed` report ledger updates (native trigger writes)? It might, but I won't bind anything on the ledger table, so it doesn't matter. The row-changed fires I care about:
- shipments (for nothing? Actually I don't need any binding on shipments if native triggers maintain the ledger!) 
- couriers (for completion write) — the courier's UPDATE status='done' is a DIRECT worker mutation → row-changed fires with table=couriers, op=update. 
- completion (for my wake) — the completion row is written by... whom?

## Completion mechanics

The completion row must be written when all three couriers are done, exactly one row, and my wake must fire exactly once.

Writer options:
A. Native SQL trigger on couriers:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS receiving_d67d641f_completion_trg
AFTER UPDATE OF status ON receiving_d67d641f_couriers
WHEN (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM receiving_d67d641f_couriers WHERE status = 'done') = 3
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM receiving_d67d641f_completion)
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO receiving_d67d641f_completion (id, completed_at) VALUES (1, datetime('now'));
END;
```
This writes the completion row when the last courier flips to done. BUT — will the engine's row-changed trigger see this INSERT (a native trigger write) so my wake fires? Uncertain! The row-changed description says "Reports only mutations made THROUGH this worker — not change data capture." A native SQL trigger executing as part of a statement issued through the worker... is it "made through this worker"? It's part of the same statement execution. Honestly it depends on implementation — some implementations hook the driver's changes API (would include trigger writes), others parse the statement (would not). SQLite's `sqlite3_changes()` counts rows changed by triggers too (it counts rows modified by the most recent statement INCLUDING trigger effects). So if the worker uses sqlite3_changes for affected_rows, the trigger insert would be included. But does the row-changed fire per table? If the worker parses the SQL statement to determine the table ("couriers"), the trigger's insert into completion wouldn't be attributed to completion table.

RISK: if row-changed doesn't attribute native trigger writes to the completion table, my wake never fires → run stalls. I MUST test this.

B. Engine binding on couriers row-changed → call database::execute with a conditional INSERT into completion (guarded by WHERE count=3 AND NOT EXISTS). This write is a DIRECT worker mutation (database::execute called by the binding) → row-changed on completion WILL fire (definitely captured, since it's a literal INSERT INTO completion through the worker). Then my wake on completion fires once.

Option B is robust for the wake. The conditional INSERT:
```sql
INSERT INTO receiving_d67d641f_completion (id, completed_at)
SELECT 1, datetime('now')
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM receiving_d67d641f_couriers WHERE status = 'done') = 3
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM receiving_d67d641f_completion);
```
- If count < 3: SELECT returns 0 rows → INSERT affects 0 rows → no error, no row. The binding fires per courier update but inserts nothing until the 3rd. Each fire is a token-free mechanical call.
- If count == 3 and no completion row: inserts exactly one row. Any subsequent fire (there won't be, since couriers update only once) would insert 0 rows due to NOT EXISTS + PK conflict would be avoided by NOT EXISTS.

So the completion row is guaranteed written by a direct worker mutation → row-changed on completion fires → my wake (once: true) fires exactly once. 

Now — will the couriers' status updates each fire row-changed on couriers? The courier does UPDATE couriers SET status='done' — direct worker mutation → fires with table=couriers, op=update. Yes.

But wait: should I ALSO handle the case where the courier inserts its couriers row with status='working'? That's an insert (op=insert) — my binding filters ops=[update], so it won't fire on insert. I'll filter ops: ["update"] to only react to the done-signal.

Actually — even simpler: the courier could insert its courier row directly with status='done' at the end. But then it's an insert op, not update. Hmm, "signal that it is finished" — either works. Let me have the courier:
1. Create its couriers row with status='working' (or 'started') at the start? Or just at the end UPDATE to 'done'. 

Actually, minimal approach: courier does its 3 inserts + correction, then `INSERT INTO couriers (supplier, status) VALUES (?, 'done')` — but if the courier row doesn't exist yet, INSERT works. Then op=insert. My completion binding could filter ops=[insert, update] or just omit ops filter but table=couriers. Hmm — but I want to avoid firing on the initial 'working' insert if I do one.

Cleanest: courier at the END does `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO couriers (supplier, status) VALUES (?, 'done')` or an UPSERT. Or simplest: UPDATE after inserting a 'working' row first. Let me decide: the courier's task:
1. Insert 3 shipment rows (in one transaction).
2. Update seq-2 value += 1.0.
3. Signal finished: UPSERT couriers (supplier, 'done').

If the courier never inserts a 'working' row, the UPSERT is an insert op. I'll filter the completion binding on ops=[insert, update] and table=couriers — but then ANY courier row insert (the very first courier to finish) fires, and the conditional SQL checks count==3. Fine — no completion until all 3 done. And the wake binding is on table=completion (not couriers), so those courier fires never wake me.

Actually wait — there's a subtle race: two couriers finishing simultaneously? They're independent sub-agents; each does its UPSERT. Each UPSERT fires row-changed → each fire runs the conditional INSERT. The SQL's count check + NOT EXISTS is atomic within a single statement in SQLite (single connection? the pool has max 10 connections, but each statement is atomic in SQLite). If two conditional INSERTs run "concurrently" on different pool connections, SQLite serializes writes (database-level lock), so one commits first, the other sees NOT EXISTS false → 0 rows. Exactly one row. 

Now — hmm, actually wait. Do I even need the completion write to be via engine binding? What if I use a native SQL trigger for completion (option A) AND test whether row-changed sees it? If it works, even fewer moving parts. But testing costs turns and there's residual risk. Option B's robustness (direct worker mutation) is worth it. Actually, let me combine: use B (engine binding → conditional insert). It's clean and guaranteed.

Hmm, but actually — wait. Let me reconsider using native SQL triggers for the completion AND relying on the wake on the completion table. The wake binding fires when row-changed on completion occurs. If native-trigger writes aren't captured, no fire. Test would be needed. Option B avoids the test. Go with B.

## Ledger: native SQL trigger vs engine binding

Native SQL trigger for ledger:
- Pros: atomic with the write, no async lag, no binding machinery, database-maintained ("live ledger ... kept current as data lands" — literally the database doing it).
- Cons: none significant. The row-changed engine trigger on shipments (if any) doesn't matter.

Wait, one more consideration: do I need ANY engine binding on shipments? No. The ledger is maintained by native triggers. The courier writes trigger the ledger updates automatically. 

But actually, hold on — let me reconsider whether native SQL triggers are "allowed" as the ONLY shared medium. "The ONLY shared medium in this run is database `primary` plus trigger machinery on top of it." Native SQL triggers are INSIDE database primary — they're part of the database, not a separate medium. And "cleanup means retiring bindings and database triggers" — the task explicitly anticipates database triggers exist. So native triggers are fine and expected.

Actually, let me reconsider the ledger approach once more. There's a question of whether the ledger must be updated by the SAME transaction as the shipment insert (native trigger does that) or can lag (engine binding). Native is strictly better here. And it doesn't run a model turn per change. 

But hmm — the phrase "kept current as data lands WITHOUT running a model turn for each change" — both approaches satisfy this. Native triggers are simpler and I don't need any pipe for the ledger. Let me go native.

Wait, one issue with native triggers: SQLite `AFTER UPDATE OF value` — the `OF value` column list requires the column name. `value` is a valid identifier. Fine.

Another subtlety: the INSERT trigger uses `ON CONFLICT(supplier) DO UPDATE`. If a courier re-inserts the same (supplier, seq) — PK conflict on shipments, not on ledger. The ledger UPSERT handles existing supplier. Fine.

Edge: What if a shipment row is inserted twice (same supplier/seq)? PK violation on shipments → the whole statement fails → trigger doesn't fire (SQLite triggers roll back with the statement). Fine.

## Courier sub-agents

Spawn 3 children:
- session_id: "receiving-d67d641f-acme" (exactly as given), "receiving-d67d641f-globex", "receiving-d67d641f-initech".
- Task: record 3 shipments into receiving_d67d641f_shipments in db "primary" (values per supplier), apply correction +1.0 to seq-2, then signal finished by setting courier row status='done'. Report nothing back; outcome is recorded in the database.
- options.functions.allow: narrow to database functions only. Child needs: engine::functions::list + engine::functions::info (always kept, per docs — "Contract discovery is never lost to narrowing — every child keeps engine::functions::list and engine::functions::info"), plus database::execute (and maybe database::transaction). Actually the child needs to run its writes — database::execute is enough; I can give it database::execute and database::transaction and database::query? Minimal: database::execute. Let me think about what the child does:
  1. Insert 3 shipments: can be one database::execute with multi-row INSERT ... VALUES (...),(...),(...) — or database::transaction with 3 statements. Simplest: one execute with a multi-VALUES insert. Or executeBatch. Actually a single INSERT with 3 value tuples is one statement — good, and the native trigger fires once per row... wait, does the SQLite trigger fire per row within a multi-row INSERT? functions.description: Read a configuration by id. Expands ${VAR:default} placeholders against the live process env unless raw=true is passed.
List every registered configuration with id, name, description, and schema. Sorted by id; never returns the stored value.

Register a configuration id with a name, description, and JSON Schema. Idempotent — re-registering replaces metadata and (when initial_value is provided) the value. Validates initial_value against the schema.
Retrieve the schema, name, and description for a configuration id. Mirrors a single entry from configuration::list.
Replace the value of an already-registered configuration. Validates the value against the registered JSON Schema and emits a configuration:updated event.
Estimate token usage for a set of messages (+ optional invocation schemas / system prompt) vs a model.
Replace verbose function outputs with placeholders without summarising. A cheaper first pass before compaction.
Internal: reload cron configuration from the authoritative store on change.
Open an interactive transaction; returns a handle to use with transactionQuery/transactionExecute/commitTransaction/rollbackTransaction.

Read a table page by page with typed filters and sorts, without writing SQL. Filters are structured (column, op, value) and compile to a parameterised WHERE for the driver in hand; the total honours the same filters. Use an equality filter at page_size 1 to follow a foreign key.

Profile a table's columns. Reads the planner's own statistics by default, which is free and approximate; `exact` runs real aggregates and scans the table. To profile rows you already hold, pipe a browseTable result through the fp worker instead.
Commit and finalize an interactive transaction.
Delete a saved query by id or by name.

Describe every table at once — the same shape as describeTable, but one catalog query per aspect across the whole database instead of one call per table. Use this to reason about relationships; set include_indexes only when you need them.

Describe one table or view: columns with type, nullability, default, primary-key membership and foreign-key target; plus indexes and a planner row estimate. Foreign keys are structured (schema, table, column), not a joined string.
Run a write statement (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL).
Run an ordered batch of SQL statements atomically (bare strings or {sql, params} objects); rolls back on first failure.

Return a statement's query plan as a tree with per-node costs, row estimates and warnings, instead of the driver's raw text. `analyze` collects real timings by RUNNING the statement, so it defaults to false and is refused for anything that is not a single read.

How a table is laid out for reading: column widths, hidden columns and column order. Stored in the state worker rather than a browser, so it survives a restart and any caller can set it up for someone else.

Live pool occupancy plus active queries, table sizes, blocking locks and cache hit ratio. Each section reports separately as available, unsupported or denied, so a driver gap or a restricted role is never mistaken for an empty result.

Recent queries run against a database, newest first. Best effort — recording never blocks or fails a query, so this is a convenience rather than an audit log. For an audit trail bind database::row-changed.
List all configured databases with connection details (driver, credential-redacted URL, pool settings, TLS mode). Config only — no health checks or live pool statistics.
List the saved queries for a database, sorted by name.
List every table and view in a database, with its kind and (on postgres) its schema. Reads the driver's own catalog, so no dialect-specific SQL is needed from the caller.
Internal: reload connection pools from the authoritative configuration when it changes.
Prepare a parameterized statement once.
Run a read-only SQL query and return the result rows.
Rollback and finalize an interactive transaction.
Run a previously-prepared handle.
Save a named query against a database. Stored in the state worker, so it survives restarts and an agent can save one for a human to find in the console. Saving under an existing name replaces it.

Replace the stored layout for a table. Widths are clamped to a usable range; columns the table no longer has are kept rather than rejected, so a rename degrades to a missing width instead of an error.

Lay out the schema as a diagram: positioned table nodes and routed foreign-key edges, plus the hub degree of each table, the isolated tables, and the remaining edge crossings. Reads the whole catalog in a handful of queries rather than one per table.
Terminate a backend session, or cancel just its running statement with `cancel_only`. Takes an id from database::health. Separate from health because it is a write.
Probe a candidate database config (url + optional tls) with one throwaway connection, without touching configured pools. Reports ok/driver/latency/server version; failures are data, not errors.
Run a sequence of statements atomically.
Run a write statement inside an interactive transaction. BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK are rejected; use commit/rollbackTransaction.
Run a read-only SQL query inside an interactive transaction.
Full detail for one engine function: schemas, owning worker, and registered triggers that target it. Proxies to the engine's native engine::functions::info for the core data.
Fetch one filesystem-backed prompt by name. Returns the raw markdown body plus name, description, and modified_at — no envelope, no templating.
List filesystem-backed prompts (name, description, modified_at) from skills_folder.

Overwrite one EXISTING filesystem-backed prompt with new full-file markdown content. The frontmatter must keep a non-empty `description` (and a valid `name` when it declares one) — the same rules the scanner enforces, so an update can never produce a file the next directory::prompts::list would skip. The write is atomic and fans out directory::prompts::on-change with { op: "update" }. Returns the prompt's effective name after the write (frontmatter `name:` wins over the file stem).

Fetch full registry metadata for one worker: worker envelope (same core fields as the engine's `engine::workers::list` row shape, plus registry-only `type` / `config` / `supported_targets` / `total_downloads` / `dependencies` / `image`), readme, full API reference (functions + triggers schemas), and the tree of skill / prompt file paths fetched from the registry's /w/{slug}/skills endpoint. Pass either `version` or `tag` (defaults to tag="latest"). Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms`.

List workers from the public registry (api.workers.iii.dev). Optional free-text `search` is matched fuzzily by the registry; omit it to browse by `total_downloads DESC`. Pagination is cursor-based with a server-authored page size — pass back `pagination.next_cursor` as `cursor` to fetch the next page. Shares the core `name` / `description` / `version` fields with the engine's `engine::workers::list`. Results are cached for `registry_cache_ttl_ms` (default 60s).

Download skills + prompts into skills_folder from EITHER source. Prefer the explicit directory::skills::download_from_registry / directory::skills::download_from_repo, whose schemas can't be mixed up. Pass {repo, skill, branch?} to clone one skill folder from a GitHub repo (branch defaults to "main"), or {worker, version?|tag?} to pull from the workers registry (tag defaults to "latest"). Specify exactly ONE source set. Files in the destination namespace are overwritten file-by-file.

Download one worker's skills + prompts from the workers registry into skills_folder. `worker` is required; pass either `version` (exact semver) OR `tag` (e.g. "latest", the default when both are omitted), not both. Files in the destination namespace are overwritten file-by-file. A missing worker returns a `D310 not_found` naming the next function to call. To pull from a GitHub repo instead, use directory::skills::download_from_repo.

Download one skill folder from a GitHub repo into skills_folder. `repo` (the repo URL) and `skill` (the subfolder under `skills/`, which also names the destination namespace) are required; `branch` defaults to "main". The repo URL is validated (https / ssh / git@ only). To pull a published worker instead, use directory::skills::download_from_registry.

Fetch one filesystem-backed skill by id and return its raw markdown body plus id, title, type, function_id, and modified_at. A worker overview is addressed by the bare worker name (e.g. "iii-sandbox") — that is the id `list`/`index` hand back. Input is forgiving: "iii-sandbox/index", "iii-sandbox/SKILL.md", a trailing ".md", and an iii:// prefix all resolve to the same overview; and if the exact id misses, the worker name is matched case-insensitively as a substring ("sandbox" finds "iii-sandbox"). `title` prefers frontmatter `title:` over the body H1; `type` is the frontmatter `type:`. There is no `description` field here (the body already opens with that paragraph) — use directory::skills::list for the teaser-only view. On a miss you get a `D110 not_found` message naming the closest ids and the next function to call.

Render a per-WORKER overview: one short markdown block per installed worker (each worker's root overview doc `<ns>/index`, whether or not it declares frontmatter `type: index`). Each block is a `## <worker title>` heading, the first paragraph of that worker's overview, and a `directory::skills::get` call to read the full reference. Token-light by design and intended for system-prompt injection; for individual per-SKILL rows call directory::skills::list.

List skills as one row PER SKILL (id, title, type, function_id, description, bytes, modified_at) from skills_folder — use this when you need individual skill ids. A worker overview row's `id` is the bare worker name (e.g. `iii-sandbox`); pass it straight to directory::skills::get. For a per-WORKER overview instead, call directory::skills::index. Filters: `search` (case-insens. substring vs id+title+description), `prefix` (worker-namespace prefix; matches the overview row and its sub-skills), `type` (exact frontmatter type match). Pass `include_description: false` for token-light id+title+type rows (default: descriptions included). `title` prefers frontmatter `title:` over the body H1. Each row's `function_id` is the callable bus id (e.g. `sandbox::create`) — pass THAT to agent_trigger, not the row's `id` (which is a documentation address).

Overwrite one EXISTING filesystem-backed skill with new full-file markdown content (frontmatter block included — pass back the `raw` field from directory::skills::get { raw: true }, edited). Accepts the same id forms as `get`. Never creates files (use directory::skills::download to materialize a bundle). Content is validated against the read invariants (size cap, non-empty body after frontmatter); the write is atomic and fans out directory::skills::on-change with { op: "update" }.
Browse DLQ messages
List DLQ topics with counts
Internal provider for TriggerAction::Enqueue
List all queue topics
Get stats for a queue topic

Remove null elements from an array (lodash _.compact, null-only: 0, false and "" are KEPT so plucked data survives): { value }. Pairs with fp::map, whose sporadic misses become null. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Trigger-binding guard: compare a JSON pointer inside the fired event and answer the condition contract ({ decision: "allow" | "skip", reason }). Config is { path?, op, to?, negate? } with the fp::when ops (==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty); a pointer that resolves to nothing SKIPS rather than erroring, so "not there yet" is an ordinary answer. Use it as a binding's `conditions` entry so a reaction fires only on events that matter — it is not a fan-in gate (that is state::barrier), it filters one event at a time.

Count array elements per plucked key (lodash _.countBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": <count> } (`""` counts by the element itself). Same key rules as fp::groupBy. Pair with fp::groupBy + fp::sum for a per-key total. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Skip the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.drop): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Keep array elements whose properties equal a partial object (lodash _.filter with a matches iteratee): { value, matches: { status: "active" } }. matches is a partial OBJECT (never a bare string/number) and only object elements can match. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Flatten an array one level (lodash _.flatten): [1,[2],[[3]]] -> [1,2,[3]]. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the single value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.get): { value, path: "/content" }. A miss names the keys that were available. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Extract the value at a JSON pointer, or `default` when the path misses (lodash fp.getOr): { value, path, default }. A stored null is a hit, not a miss. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Bucket array elements by a plucked key (lodash _.groupBy): { value, path: "/writer" } -> { "<key>": [element, ...] } (`""` groups by the element itself). Keys must be a string, number, or boolean; a null or container key errors rather than collapsing distinct groups into one bucket. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Join array elements into one string (lodash _.join): { value, separator } (separator defaults to ","). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Pluck the value at a JSON pointer from each array element (lodash _.map with a property iteratee): { value, path: "/id" }. Sporadic misses become null (fp::compact drops them), but a path matching NO element errors — pointers pluck stored fields, not computed properties like /length (fp::size counts). Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Largest number in an array (lodash _.max/_.maxBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.maxBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Arithmetic mean of an array of numbers (lodash _.mean/_.meanBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/score" }. Deviates from lodash: an EMPTY array errors instead of yielding NaN, which would thread garbage into the next step. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Smallest number in an array (lodash _.min/_.minBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" }. Deviates from lodash _.minBy: returns the NUMBER, not the element holding it, so a fp::when guard can compare it directly. An empty array errors. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Element at index n; negative n counts from the end (lodash _.nth): { value, n: -1 } is the last element. Out of bounds errors naming the length. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Drop top-level keys from an object (lodash _.omit): { value, paths: ["a","b"] }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Subset an object by top-level keys (lodash _.pick): { value, paths: ["a","b"] } -> {a, b}; missing keys are omitted. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Run a short worker-side pipeline in one call: each step triggers a function and its result lands in the next step's payload at `into` (default "/value") — large values flow worker→worker and never enter the chat. fp::* transform steps (get/pick/omit/take/drop/map/filter/split/join/uniq/size/compact/nth/getOr/flatten/sortBy/reverse/when, lodash semantics) run inline and thread the transformed value itself — the {value} wrapper they return when called directly never appears between steps. A failing fp::when guard STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step runs only when its condition holds. The FIRST step receives no threaded value: start with a producing function (a fetch, a state::get) or seed a leading transform via payload.value. Example: fetch an article and persist it trimmed: through=[{function:'scrapling::fetch', payload:{url,format:'markdown'}}, {function:'fp::get', payload:{path:'/content'}}, {function:'fp::take', payload:{n:20000}}, {function:'state::set', payload:{scope,key}}]. Returns per-step sizes and a preview, not the value. shell::*/coder::* steps run under the session's harness-stamped filesystem scope; without one (no working directory, or a non-harness caller) they are refused — call them directly instead. Database write steps are refused only while `approval::gate` is registered.
Reverse an array (lodash _.reverse, immutable like lodash/fp): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Count a collection (lodash _.size): array length, string chars, or object key count: { value }. Non-collections error instead of returning 0. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Sort array elements ascending by the value at a JSON pointer (lodash _.sortBy, stable): { value, path } — path "" sorts the elements themselves (primitives). Keys must all be numbers, strings, or booleans; an element missing the path errors. Pair with fp::reverse for descending. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Split a string into an array of strings (lodash _.split): { value, separator: "\n" }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Total an array of numbers (lodash _.sum/_.sumBy): { value }, or { value, path: "/amount" } to pluck the addend from each element first. An empty array totals 0; a non-numeric element errors rather than being skipped. All-integer inputs total to an integer, so the result compares cleanly in a fp::when guard. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Keep the first n elements of an array or the first n characters of a string (lodash _.take): { value, n }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.
Deduplicate an array, keeping first occurrences (lodash _.uniq): { value }. Mainly useful as a fp::pipe step.

Guard: test the value at a JSON pointer ({ value, path?, op, to? }; ops ==, !=, >, >=, <, <=, exists, not_empty; path defaults to the whole value; a pointer miss FAILS the guard, it never errors). Direct calls return { passed, value }. As a fp::pipe step, a passing guard threads the ORIGINAL value onward unchanged and a failing one STOPS the pipe (`short_circuited: true`), so a trailing write step (e.g. state::set) runs only when the condition holds.
Aggregate durable model usage, function outcomes, and available trace/span observability. `complete` is true only after every session in the durable tree has reached a terminal turn.
Read the durable root-and-descendant session tree for one harness run.

Spawn a sub-agent in a child session (direct call only — never a trigger target). Fire-and-forget: returns { child_session_id, child_turn_id } immediately; the child's outcome reaches you only through whatever destination its task names. The child is a LEAF by default (no spawn/send/trigger registration); pass options.orchestrator: true to grant the orchestration surface, still capped by the caller's own policy. The task must include literal values for every required resource selector (for example `db: "primary"`). Omit child `max_turns` unless its budget covers discovery, contract lookup, work, and the deliverable.
Read the current turn status for a session.

Read-only: the trigger bindings a session owns (durable records) — subscription id, trigger type/config, delivery target (absent = notifies the owner), conditions, lifecycle, and fire count. In-turn agent calls may omit `session_id` (defaults to the calling session).

Tear down one trigger binding by subscription id: unregister the engine trigger AND delete the durable record (an engine-side unregister alone strands the owner's armed wake). `session_id` must name the binding's owner; in-turn agent calls may omit it (defaults to the calling session). A still-armed wake torn down this way notifies its parked owner.
Enqueue a message
Discard (purge) a single DLQ message by ID
Redrive all DLQ messages back to the main queue
Redrive a single DLQ message by ID back to the main queue
Define and start a durable named function queue
Internal: reload queue configuration from the authoritative store.
Read one catalog model by {provider, id}; null when the model is not registered.
List catalog models, optionally filtered by provider and/or a capability flag.
Check whether a model supports a capability flag (fails open for unknown models).
List registered providers with their configured/available status.
Read one session's metadata (null when unknown).
Read a single entry by id (null when unknown).
List sessions with pagination, ordering, and status/metadata filters.
Load the active path as messages with entry ids, oldest first; pagination and role filtering.
Delete a value from a stream
Get a value from a stream
List all items in a stream group
List all available stream with metadata
List all groups in a stream
Send a custom event to stream subscribers
Set a value in a stream
Atomically update a stream value with multiple operations

Install a worker from a registry slug, an OCI image ref, or a LOCAL project directory (one containing an iii.worker.yaml). Call worker::schema to see each source shape, and worker::validate to dry-run an iii.worker.yaml before installing. LOCAL installs run the project directory LIVE and start a source watcher: code edits auto-restart the worker, so do NOT re-add after changing source files — re-add (force: true) only when iii.worker.yaml itself changes. Installs can outlive a bus invocation timeout and CONTINUE server-side — on timeout, poll worker::status instead of re-issuing (the project lock stays held until the in-flight install finishes).
Wipe worker artifacts
List installed workers
Read a worker's recent stdout/stderr log lines from the engine host. `tail` bounds lines per stream (default 100, max 1000).
Uninstall workers and clear their artifacts
Introspect request/response schemas for worker::* triggers. Optional `function_id` filters to a single trigger. Also serves the iii.worker.yaml manifest schema under the pseudo-id "iii.worker.yaml".
Start a configured worker

Install/runtime status for ONE worker: installed?, running?, pid, version, a sanitized recent log tail, and a next-step hint. THE poll target after worker::add { wait: false } or after an add/update call hit a bus timeout (the install keeps running server-side).
Stop a running worker

Reinstall REGISTRY-installed workers preserving config (re-resolves iii.lock pins). LOCAL-path workers are NOT touched by this: their source watcher already auto-restarts them on code edits; only an iii.worker.yaml change needs worker::add with force: true. Like worker::add, updates can outlive a bus timeout and continue server-side — poll worker::status.

Dry-run validation of an iii.worker.yaml WITHOUT installing anything. Pass `manifest` (inline YAML text) or `path` (host file/dir). Returns errors, unknown keys, deprecated keys, and warnings — author, validate, then worker::add.

Stream leave trigger

One-shot deadline: fires exactly once at `at` (epoch ms). Register with { "in_ms": <relative ms> } — resolved to an absolute `at` at registration — or { "at": <epoch ms> }. The natural second leg of any armed wake or fan-in gate: 'wake me when X happens, or tell me at T that it did not'. Fires once and retires; for recurrence use `cron`.
Trace/span event trigger
Worker lifecycle events emitted by every worker::* op. Subscribe with `operations` / `stages` / `workers` filters.
